I adore this game. I've played it off and on since it was released in 2017. The stories in this game are full of interesting lore and quests that add depth to this unnerving massive underground room. You play as a train driver that drives through various rooms to locate a way out of the "House." Along the way you recruit people to your train's staff as well as solve mysteries for those in the various cities you encounter. Each region of the House has it's own enemies and secrets to uncover. 

Combat involves trains basically shooting their ammunition at each other. The game shows the two trains next to each other from a top-down perspective so you can see the stations and rooms in the train. This lets you direct your people on where to go for repair and where to shoot the enemy. One can aim the cannons but whether the accuracy is high enough depends on the installed weapons and any upgrades. I personally tried to avoid combat since that wasn't as interesting as exploring and uncovering stories.

The way this game projects a creeping horror is so well done. I also like how the attributes play a role in achieving one's goal or not (such as if Guile is too low, a test of Guile may be very difficult to overcome. In that case I may either risk the consequences of failing or back out to try again after I raised my Guile. Note that some decisions cannot be backed out of and returned to later). 

Overall, for a creepy horror game, it's well worth the adventure. Can you find a way out of the House? Or will you be left wandering its halls forever?

A House of Many Doors' gameplay is admittedly, very jank. Mostly it consists of trundling through empty rooms, on and on, to get to your next destination. The combat is worse, the mix of turn-based and real-time making it somehow both boringly slow moving and requiring incredibly fast reflexes. And all of this is compounded by the game's innumerable bugs, imbalances, and unintentional loopholes.

Why then is A House of Many Doors one of my favourite games of all time?

The obvious answer would be to say the game's luscious worldbuilding. Each location is described with strange yet perfectly clear imagery, the world is very well developed but it never feels like the game is simply dropping exposition on the player's head, and so much feels unique and different compared to the standard fantasy tropes that define the genre. This world building is definitely what drew me to A House of Many Doors in the first place. But if we compare it to its direct inspirations, the games in the Fallen London universe, particularly Sunless Sea, these games are just as successful in their worldbuilding -- and yet I think A House of Many Doors surpasses even these.

What I think really makes this game succeed is in its cohesion and structure. The problem I have with the Sunless games is that while they are in theory at least about the player character's unquenchable ambition -- a central plot thread that the player character will pursue at any cost -- in truth, these ambitions are the least interesting parts of the games (with perhaps the exception of Sunless Skies' Martyr King's Cup, which surprise, surprise is in fact written by Harry Tuffs, the writer behind A House of Many Doors). In contrast, A House of Many Doors main quest is not only incredibly interesting, but is also mechanically and narratively tied to the game's sidequests. To progress in the main plot, you need to explore and complete sidequests, and ultimately this then positions you to make the difficult choices that the plot demands. Through exploring the House, the player gains the insight necessary to decide its fate. Everything fits together into a compelling and thematic whole.

I would definitely recommend A House of Many Doors if you enjoy narrative heavy games and don't mind the slower pace. There is an overlapping audience with fans of the Fallen London games, but A House of Many Doors is a lot less bleak and unforgiving, so even if you don't enjoy those games, it might be worth giving this one a go.

A House of Many Doors is a game I've loved for ages, so it's where I'm going to start with my new project of "review more games in my library".

I'll be honest, this game can be a slog. I am a person who can easily put on a podcast in order to do boring game tasks like "crawling from city to city in a largely fixed and repetitive map"; I am also a person who puts in the effort to make a map in a spreadsheet to make playing the game easier. The vehicle-to-vehicle combat minigame is difficult to master, and there's a LOT of clicking through storyline options in a city and little tasks to attend to (I do also enjoy little tasks).

That said? The game was made by one guy doing frankly unsustainable levels of work, and the art and writing captivate me so intensely I will overlook the boring travel parts in order to dive into the beautiful, offbeat, cynical, deeply humanist stories the game conjures. Each location and each person commits to its strangeness wholeheartedly, and the patchwork creates a whole world as diverse, cruel, and marvelous as our own. It reminds me of a lazy spring afternoon hauling a tabletop role-playing sourcebook into the tree outside my house when I was twelve and getting lost in someplace else, with a far clearer-headed attitude towards power and living in systems of power than most, and for that, I'll overlook any fault.

I love Failbetter Games' "Fallen London" and this game desperately wants to be that, but I quit after the first combat. This game has a great premise but is just not fun to play and starts you off hopelessly lost.

It's a bit rough around the edges, but this is an [i]amazing[/i] gem of interactive fiction. If you played Sunless Seas and/or Sunless Skies and want "more of that but different" -- a (different) incomprehensibly weird world full of strange places to explore and even weirder creatures to meet -- this game is exactly that. There are literally dozens, maybe over a hundred unique Weird Places to go visit! And in all those places are countless unimaginable experiences, from befriending a tribe of word-hunters to romancing ten million crows.

I hesitate to directly compare them against each other, but at times I find A House of Many Doors actually has [i]stronger[/i] writing than Failbetter's work, though that may simply be because it's a one-writer project, so the overall feeling is a bit more cohesive. Catherine Unger's art is also incredibly evocative and really adds to the already-wonderful writing.

It's not perfect, and be prepared to encounter many bugs, a few design weirdnesses, and so forth. As a result, I'd say it might be a bit less accessible than Sunless Seas/Skies, so it's probably easier to wrap your head around if you've played those first.

One of my favorite games of all time, and now recommendable to others with the recent patches and bug fixes. If you like classic CRPG-style role-playing, Sunless Sea or Escape Velocity, Lovecraft, subtle political, cultural and philosophical commentary, and self-aware pretentiousness, this is the game for you. The writing is incredible; the settings are clever and thoroughly inspired; the art unique and lovely; and the vision uncompromising and vast, yet cogent and scrutable. It is a game that has made a penetrating impact on my creative sensibility and personal cosmological outlook. The psychedelic and bohemian references are also subtle and thoroughly appreciated.

The grind is in the exploration, given the absolute ease of save-scumming and the limited FTL-style combat. A lot of people hate this, but it's ultimately the work that makes the discoveries and stories worth it. Until you start to understand the meta of the game and unlock reliable money-making operations (things kept intentionally oblique early on), every discovery and new interaction feels novel and potentially consequential, and this effect is under-girded by the empty space in-between events. This game also has a lot to say about Emptiness as a spiritual and philosophical concept, and the emptiness in the game is (I think) an important aesthetic and mechanical aspect of that theme's presentation.

This game has some of the best written prose out of any narrative game I've played. If you enjoy narrative-heavy games like Sunless Sea/Skies or Disco Elysium, this game easily fits up there with them. Many of the other reviews talk about buggy/poor gameplay, which was sort of true. While I personally think the game was worth playing in its entirety since it first released, I could understand why some people found the game tedious or unenjoyable. My main advice for people picking up the game would be to change the text size from medium to large or extra large right at the beginning. If you like reading about an expansive, developed world full of everything bizarre, dark, and otherworldly, this is definitely a game to play through multiple times.

A game in a similar vein to [i]Sunless Sea[/i], with a core setting premise unlike what any other games we've seen have really attempted, and a generally fascinating approach to causality, morality, and all sorts of other things up to and of course including the laws of physics — not necessarily in ways the player can interact with, mind you, a lot of it will just be something you read in a one-off event that leaves you with food for thought for a while, but appreciated all the same. The basic gameplay loop is pretty simple: you drive your train-on-legs through a series of rooms with randomly-generated obstacles, encounters, and/or enemies, and ferry goods between the various persistent locations (generally cities and the like). And if that's what you're interested in, there are better games for it; the draw, here, is more about the snippets of lore you uncover and the bizarre missions and sometimes stranger crewmates you can take on during your travels. And the major overarching plot, which we will not be spoiling here. Suffice to say, we are quite fond of it.

The setting, narrative, characters, atmosphere, and general writing quality are all quite good, but the game mechanics themselves leave somewhat to be desired — which is something that the update released today is intended to help with; haven't had a chance to really delve into and properly experience how much has changed yet, so that'll have to be left for a later edit of this review.

This is one of the weirder games I have in my steam library, and one of the ones I least regret buying. There's a lot of jank and unfinished content, which is to be expected of a game as expansive as this being coded and written by a single person, and it presents a very niche style of gameplay - one I've only seen Sunless Sea and Sunless Skies do, the former being referred to by the sole developer as a very big inspiration, and his work on HOMD resulting in him being hired by that game's studio to write content for the latter of the two. 

It can and will get very repetitive to slog through however, especially as enough of the map and the location of key points are discovered as navigation becomes as easy as counting the shortest number of cells between A and B, and I wouldn't recommend it if holding forward between time spent reading doesn't sound like an appealing gameplay loop, but the strength of the writing and the sheer novelty of the bizarre worldbuilding and cosmology of the setting do a lot to support the otherwise barebones frame of movement between locations. Very few other games let you attend a vampire's AA meeting, or coerce fungi to unionize, or woo a city's polluted river with wine, or romance an amalgamation of millions of crows stitched together by some force, or use your heart as a flashlight.

The monotony that otherwise can set in is broken up by moments like these, and with crew content which might have certain triggers unlocked while scuttling from place to place, or skirting around aggressive enemies. Sunless Sea and especially Sunless Skies have a lot more player stimulation if you want something akin to this style of gameplay that's more fleshed-out and visually varied. But as someone who's played the ♥♥♥♥ out of both and was a kickstarter backer for Sunless Skies, I've very biased towards these kinds of games.

It's weird and I love it for it. Every location feels unsettling in its own unique way, and rarely does there seem to be any banality when a new location is discovered. Oddwinter and Station Null in particular baffled me on my first playthrough ages ago, when trying to piece together what the House is and how it operates.

I'd recommend trying it with the unofficial patch installed to restore cut content and crew members, as well as skimming a transcript of the developer's AMA posted in the community hub's forums, if you're interested in their (incorrect) opinions on how ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ shark-people are when writing dialogue, or their creative process behind some of the weirder elements of the game's lore and setting.

Honestly, my feelings about this game are too complex to put into words. They're all very positive though, and with the amount it goes on sale for, it is undoubtedly worth it. I'll probably play it again for another ending at some point.

The writing, story, and world-building in this game are utterly fantastic. Truly my favorite game of all time. It has its flaws, and it's definitely not for everyone, but I find it better than sunless sea in many regards. If you like the supernatural, high concept science fiction, and wonderfully written characters, this game is absolutely worth trying.
very good. Kinda repeatitive but very good.
The setting is so good, I regularly find myself excited to push the story forward.
Similar vibe to Sunless Skies. The visuals, music and general playability isn't as good, but the stories are excellent and well worth the minor irritations.

The writing is great. I wish that this whole game was just that.

Sadly, it also has combat. Which makes zero sense, is not at all explained, there are no decent guides for it, and frankly as far as I can figure out that's because it makes sense to nobody. Just completely ruins a well-written story.

The game shares a lot of similarities with Sunless Seas/Skies including the procedural layout, emphasis on creating and maintaining a large vessel, collecting an eclectic cast of officers that each have their own stories, and reliance on what could be best described as intense metaphysical pulp writing. However, the way that it is presented in HoMD is unique enough that calling it a clone would be disparaging to both. HoMD is a rough game, but a beautiful and deep world that is filled with mysteries to uncover and oceans of stories to navigate. If you buy it, be sure to get the Unofficial Patch to help smooth out the more rough edges.

this is what happens when you have excellent writing and atrocious programming and game design. what happened here? did they sacrificed their devs to make a deal with satan, who helped the rest of the team to write? that's my head canon anyway.

the setting
that's what is great about this game. if you manage to read small font with notches (it's small even if you picked the "large" option), you will be hooked from the start. the game is unique and tries to tell a new story, in a new setting, it's not like your cookie-cutter fantasy or sci-fi.
in short, you are trapped in a strange dimension which is called "house of many doors". this place kidnaps people and bits of places from different universes and holds everything inside. the inside of the house is hundreds of square rooms with one door on an each wall. remember film "cube"? sorta like that, but each room is enormous and you are not walking through them but travel inside some steam punk mechanism that looks like a centipede. your goal is obviously to learn what's going on and how to escape. 
everything about the house is intriguing, and you probably think, yay that's one of those ocd exploration games with a plot for ages right?
well, it could be that, but all the potential is absolutely ruined by the horrors of the actual gameplay.

the gameplay
so we have big square space and want a player to explore it. let's give the people a tiny 2 centimeter thingy which can be moved by wasd but slooooowly and clunky. you can go forward or back using w and s and now probably thinking that if you want to turn left or right you'll use a and d? wrong! it's w+a and w+d! why? ♥♥♥♥ you, that's why, game will never tell anyway.
in the lower left corner the game has tiny window with the daily log. i could't read it even in my glasses. in-game day goes pretty quickly and if you are driving through one room, several days will pass for sure. god knows what was happening there, it's the same font with notches, that could't be saved even by large option, and the log window is so tiny you always have to scroll ♥♥♥♥ inside. 
in the right upper corner you can enable your crew list - the npcs that are given you by the game. there is a bigger window where you can actually read something most of the time. you can talk to you crew there, see your quests, inventory and such.
the rest of the screen is an empty black space. the rooms in the house are all like that. gigantic black space, which you are crossing in a tiny 2 centimetric object, while the tiny window on the left is blinking with the unreadable log. sometimes inside the room you'll find a random object which has a reddish glow - that's the interractable point, come close and bump in it, read the description of the event in the right window, make some choices and move on. sometimes you will find the npc in the same type centipede machine as you are, and it almost every time means you will need to fight them. this leads us to the most terrible part - 

the combat
i have no words to express how much i hated the combat. it is insanely bad. you have no idea, how bad it is.
so it's turnbased combat sequence. you will get a square filled with tiniest human icons on the left part of the screen - that's you, and  on the right - it's your enemy. the idea of it is the same like in the most strategic games - you have 4 actin points, spend it, end turn, look what it did and then look what will enemy do.
this game took that concept and filled it with agony. in short, it is absolutely unclear what to do.
btw there are some tooltips but they do not help. i don't need a tip to know that if i want to end my turn i need to press an "end turn" button, but it would be lovely to know things such as:
- although the attacking units have a special fire button, and you need to click it manually to make an attack, the support units DO NOT have it and you don't need to click any confirmation for their actions, they just need to come to the place where something needs to be healed or fixed, and they will do it automatically
- how much action can do one unit, can i just fire 4 times in a row with the same gunner? the points can be spent this way but i still can't tell if it did the thing, because there is no proper battle log, and every amount of attack looks the same
- some npcs in your square aren't playable at all, you can't command them in any way, i still have no idea why are they there in the first place.
etc.
keep in mind that you need to figure out this ♥♥♥♥ clicking by the tiniest icons imaginable, and the enemies look exactly the same as your crew, so if they hopped to your square, you will not tell the difference between them.
i repeat, i have no words to describe the level of frustration of the battle design in this game.
but the picture would not be completed without the last precious piece:

the bugs
game crashes a lot. the combat part is so buggy that  it's like half of the time something breaks and the only way to fix it is to reload. 
we will never know how to escape the damn house of many doors and what all your mysterious dreams were meaning, because it's impossible to sit through this mess.


in case you are still on the fence if you should buy it - look for the screenshots of the actual gameplay (not the artsy ones, that everyone is posting one the community hub). it is pure pain. if you want pain, play any souls title, these games at least are less buggy and have an interface not made by bunch of humanitarians who sacrificed to satan everyone from the dev department.

I tentatively recommend this game, on the premise that you've already played Sunless Sea and enjoyed that game to the fullest. This game is awesome in the same ways Sunless Sea is awesome, with a lot of cool worldbuilding and harrowing events. This game is terrible in the same ways that Sunless Sea is terrible, with terrible gameplay and even duller travels.

The balance of the gameplay is especially bad in this game. Once you get past a certain point, the risk of death in the overworld drops to zero as long as long as you just run away from every fight. Fuel becomes cheap, money easy to come by, and so travels just become this tedious waiting game filled with randomly placed, repetitive sprites. The balance of the economy in Sunless Sea still felt somewhat challenging even by the end of it.

Though if you can tolerate the tedious parts, the ending that I experienced was truly cathartic to me. And the ideas and characters along the way were all interesting, the storylines always intriguing. So yeah. Similar strengths to Sunless Sea, similar weaknesses.
This game is fantastic, the writing is on par with (and often surpasses in my opinion) Sunless Sea's writing.

Juego de rol enfocado en la narrativa, la exploración y la gestión de recursos. Es el hermano pobre y desconocido de Sunless Sea (al que supera). Estamos atrapados en una dimensión (la Casa) y buscamos la salida. Nos desplazamos en un vehículo mecánico impulsado por un corazón humano a través de las tinieblas. El mapa está dividido en casi 4000 cuadrículas (las habitaciones) patrulladas cada una de ellas por otro vehículo que nos perseguirá por regla general (nos movemos con las teclas AWSD).

Ganamos puntos de experiencia al completar misiones y descubrir nuevas localizaciones. Esos puntos se canjean para subir nuestros atributos al interactuar con los miembros de la tripulación de cubierta superior (cada uno de ellos nos ofrece una subtrama, son 30 en total). Cada lugar importante está representado por un cuadro sobre el que aparece el texto con las posibilidades que nos ofrece. No todos los asentamientos disponen de tiendas para comerciar. Son 88 localizaciones.

Una barra nos indica el combustible, otra la cordura y una tercera representa la integridad del casco del vehículo. Gastando dinero podemos recuperar cordura cuando llegamos a las ciudades. Éste se gana vendiendo información, escribiendo artículos para periódicos, invirtiendo en negocios, trasladando pasajeros y mediante la compraventa de mercancías.

El combate por turnos está poco inspirado y es mejor evitarlo (pero debemos mejorar el vehículo). La mayor parte del tiempo vas a estar leyendo (ni voces ni escenas) y explorando. Necesitas, al menos, un nivel intermedio de inglés para disfrutarlo. Es un juego independiente de nicho que -con sus evidentes defectos por falta de presupuesto- ofrece la recreación de un universo fascinante y absorbente. Narrativa ingeniosa con momentos brillantes.

Rejugable. Más de 60 misiones. Tres finales distintos. Dos niveles de dificultad. Refleja muy bien la pérdida de cordura con las anotaciones del diario, el cambio de música y como se difuminan las imágenes. Puedes guardar la partida casi en todo momento y tiene autoguardado. Posibilidad de viaje rápido entre localizaciones. Ofrece muchas sorpresas a quien se vea atrapado por su historia y tenga la paciencia suficiente.
One of the best weird fiction novels I've ever read!

If you like out-there narratives and can handle a little jank you can't go wrong with this game. It's buggy and you can see the signs from time to time that this was a one-man team with no prior gamemaking experience, but if you can handle a Bethesda game you can probably handle this. In exchange you'll get one of the best, most ambitious and most wildly entertaining stories in all of gaming. House of Many Doors is a proper diamond in the rough, and a game that's never left my thoughts ever since I first played it.

If you loved sunless sea (or lovecraftian style stories) its definitely worth a go.
Super impressive as it was a 1 dev effort

I like the premise of it. It's not as mechanically good as say, Sunless Sea, but this one did come first. I do like the story though and there's definitely some interesting stuff. Also, all hail Anglecrab.

Just a really, very good game. People compare it with Sunless Seas a lot - it's a valid comparison, as there's plenty of similarities in gameplay and setting. However, I really think this game stands on its own, and in some ways I prefer the setting and the stories within it over those in Fallen London. It's dark, mysterious to an almost Lovecraftian degree at times, and deeply compelling. Never read anything else quite like it.

The writing is what carries the game, for sure, and it's worth playing for that alone. The core gameplay is a little rough around the edges, but I still had fun with it. If you played and liked Sunless Seas, you'll feel pretty much at home. The only thing that ever made me hesitate to recommend this game was the fact that it suffered from a number of pretty serious bugs that never got patched - however, with the new unofficial patch, these are (hopefully) not an issue, and I'm deeply grateful to a stranger named "Altotas" for making it.

Just go for it, this game rules. Its setting and writing are really damn interesting, and it's extremely satisfying to explore them and learn more of what's going on. You really never know what to expect, and I find that wonderful. A+, big fan. :)

Cripplingly slow, pump every single thing you can into increasing speed and getting witch mirrors or whatever theyre called. But an incredible setting and story that to this day I think of.

A warning that there is such a thing as too much downtime. If I pull out my phone to watch videos while your game is playing,  im not thinking about what ive seen and putting things together, im just bored.

A game where you learn to drive, help people, maybe possibly probably kill innocents and steal their memories for your own gain, and make an adventure. I haven't beaten the game yet, so I can't speak to the endgame, but I love the sidequests, the depth of detail, the humor of geese being summoned and mauling people, and the characters you can help. There's so much to do that it's a bit overwhelming at first, but that just makes getting used to the game all the better. It's not easy, and it's definitely a game for people who love to gamble with the lives of fictional characters, so I'd say I love the whole thing so far.

Edit: I have beaten the game. I don't really know what to say, aside from that I feel full. I had a grand adventure, had more fun than I remember in a while, and that I can appreciate the sun now. Leaving the house I'm in means all the more after seeing but one ending. I plan to see what I have missed, and what I can do.

PLUSES
+ Writing: precise, original, humorous when it's needed, grim when you don't expect it.
+ Crew members: good characters with interests that may not align with yours.
+ Setting: a very simple, but inspiring idea about a dimension that steals whole cultures from different worlds allows for a fantastic diversity of things you can meet and explore.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who played Sunless Sea and felt like it was too long, too enigmatic and too hard to complete. I also recommend this game to anyone who played Sunless Sea and enjoyed it, although for you this game may feel too short.
In general, if like good stories and feel in the mood for some wacky exploration – try it out. I did not expect this game to be this good.


MINUSES
- IMPORTANT: The game was made by one person and wasn't well tested. Beware of bugs: usually they're minor like typos but sometimes you can get stuck in the debris and forced to reload the save file (happened to me once). Long game sessions (5h+) cause memory leaks (also happened once), some quests can bug and do not work ( happened once, I solved it reloading the game). Unofficial patch seems to help the game a lot though and the bugs aren't often.
- Mild: The exploration outside of the points of interest isn't that exciting. The same events repeat very often, all rooms look almost the same, ship control is a bit clunky and it's annoying at longer distances. However, it feels more engaging than in Sunless Sea, because it's MUCH faster and also allows you to gather a lot of valuable resources you can sell or use later. It's fine if you're warned. 
- Minor: game isn't adapted for 2K and 4K displays. The text of the game is a bit too small for me (I have 2K display).

QUESTIONABLE:
? Combat: I enjoyed this combat a lot more than SSea's. The idea is good and the implementation is fine. However, it feels a bit... lacking? It feels like it's too easy to just bully your enemy with big guns before they can do anything. But I liked quests that involved fighting, unlike the similar tasks in SSea, so try it for yourself.
This one's up there with Sunless Skies for me, even if it's scrappy.

needs more polish. menuing feels janky, which is bad for a game that is mostly menus. i have a laptop size screen that is 1080p native. at 1920x1080, text is blurry and too small to read comfortably. at lower resolutions, the ui doesnt scale so it becomes this cluttered mess of ungainly ui elements, and the text is still blurry. ive tried adjusting the usual suspects (.exe dpi options, windows scaling), and it still doesnt work.
Definitely a buggy game, and a bit slow, but some of the best worldbuilding and best writing I've seen in a game for a long time.

A House of Many Doors is a game that incorporates vivid storytelling via text with periods of top-down travel in your "kinetopede" to new locations. You're a poet/journalist on an adventure to break out or escape "The House".
I put off finishing this game for about a month because I really didn't want it to end. I did the final quest today, there are alternate decisions you can make to finalize your play through. I have never played a game before with such creative and captive writing. It was so fun to read through the quests and location descriptions within "The House". There's combat to the likes of FTL but it can be avoided nearly 100% of the time if you rather explore than fight. I would highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys reading and dark fantasy.

I honestly think this is better than sunless skies, I love the world that it created and the story it built, smart and filled with depth while being clear enough to actually progress through without selling your life to the game.

The game has flaws. There are small bugs, a clunky combat system, and innumerable little quirks and tweaks in the "game" part of the gameplay that can drive you up a wall from frustration. If you're willing to put up with those (and believe me, there's a lot to put up with), install the unofficial patch to clear up some of the others, you can find an amazingly esoteric, creepy, exotic and surreal screampunk gothic world to explore, with hidden setting details, angst, creep-show factor, cool characters with interesting backstories and motivations, and a really good creepy gothic time. Worth my time, and the price point.

It's a low budget indie take on Sunless Seas.  Unfortunately, it's so poorly done I found myself wishing I was just playing Sunless Seas, instead.

Yes, the writing and setting is there, but everything else is awful.  Rather than guiding a ship through an atmospheric continuous map, you're driving this kludgy tractor across individual map cells with crude graphics.  You soon realize that there aren't really strong biomes for the most part.  With the exception of certain enemy spawns, you'll be staring at the same crude sprites on the map repeatedly.  Oh, and there's a combat minigame too: it vaguely resembles FTL, has a completely incongruous art style to the rest of the game, and generally isn't fun.

The writing was interesting, unfortunately the dev should've just made this a CYOA/IF game, rather than try to pull off a remake of Sunless Seas.

"Still jetzt! 
Stoppt alle Maschinen, löscht das Feuer im Kessel!
Sie sind zu nah, viel zu nah...
Sie dürfen uns nicht bemerken.
Einem weiteren Angriff halten wir nicht mehr stand.
Sie kommen näher, uns bleibt keine Wahl.
Löscht auch das lodernde Licht tief im Herzen der Maschine, löscht das Herz selbst...

Es schlägt noch zweimal, leiser und leiser, dann verstummt es und Stille umfängt uns vollkommen.
Jeder verharrt auf seinem Posten, stumm und erstarrt harren wir der Dinge, die da kommen.

Draußen können wir sie hören - die Anderen. Ihre Maschine gleicht der unseren, die stählernen Beine des mechanischen Tausendfüßlers kratzen über den steinernen Boden. Das Ungetüm ist groß, zu groß, um uns auf einen Kampf einzulassen und in seinen eisernen Eingeweiden lauern die Anderen. Bis an die Zähne bewaffnet sind sie zum entern bereit, sie wollen was uns gehört, all die Schätze und Artefakte, die wir auf unseren Reisen fanden.... und die Wunder.

Die Crew ist immer noch wie erstarrt, der erste Bordschütze blickt zum Captain hinüber, doch in der Dunkelheit kann er seinen Blick nicht deuten. Er wartet ab, jeden Muskel bis zum Zerreißen gespannt.

Doch der Captain sagt kein Wort. Er hat schon zu viel erlebt, zuviel gesehen und zuviel bedauert. Wir warten in der Dunkelheit, samtweich umhüllt sie unsere Maschine. 

Doch in der Finsternis lauern die Schatten, feingliedrige Hände greifen nach uns, sie zerren an unserem Verstand, flößen uns mit fiebrigen Flüsterstimmchen düstere Gedanken ein und süß, klebriger Wahnsinn tropft von ihren rasiermesserscharfen Krallen...

Sie werden nicht fortgehen, solange das Herz der Maschine schweigt, sie werden stärker und stärker, bis... bis sie uns übermannen und wir, nicht mehr Herr unserer Sinne, in den Abgrund stürzen.

Der letzte Angriff hat uns viel gekostet, wir haben den ersten Maat verloren und unseren Arzt, es gab Verletzte und die Maschine kam ins Wanken. Tagelang lagen wir havariert in der Dunkelheit, nur das Herz pochte ohne Unterlass und hielt uns bei Sinnen.

Nun ist es ganz still und wir werden furchtsam und schwach..."

Ja, lieber Leser: So ist das, wenn man in fremden, höchst andersartigen Dimensionen auf Schatzsuche geht. Bist Du mutig genug, um es der Besatzung dieses seltsamen Gefährts gleichzutun? Halb Tausendfüßler, halb Schiff krabbelt es durch dunkle, ungezählte Räume und trägt seine tapfere Crew durch immer neue Türen in immer neue wundersame Abenteuer.

Und wenn Du Dich dabei ein wenig an Sunless Sea erinnert fühlst, dann hast Du natürlich vollkommen Recht, es spielt sich wirklich genau so. 
Und das ist ja durchaus gut so und als Kompliment gemeint. 
Du wählst Dir eine Crew aus höchst eigenwilligen Charakterköpfen aus, pflegst Deine Beziehungen zu ihnen und passt auf, dass unterwegs niemand verloren geht. 
Da wird auch mal der Kanonier für seine Sammlung von illustren Schmuddelmagazinen gerügt, oder dem Alkoholiker Steuermann der Diebstahl eines Fläschchens Flüssigtrostspenders durchgehen gelassen. Es wird gestritten, debattiert oder geflirtet und das macht das Ganze sehr lebendig und immersiv.

Und natürlich trägt Deine Crew auch was zur Reise bei, erhöht Deine Stats oder kämpft tapfer in der Schlacht. Und Die Kämpfe haben es in sich, alle Besatzungsmitglieder wollen genau platziert und eingesetzt werden, es wird geballert, geentert und geplündert, dass es eine wahre Freude ist. 

Und was bleibt dann noch übrig? Klar: Das Erforschen und Entdecken! Und das macht unglaublich Laune, in jedem Raum dieser gar wunderlichen Welt wimmelt es von Mysterien und okkulten Verrücktheiten. 
Vieles ist spannend, wertvoll oder gefährlich. Oder alles zugleich.

Klaust Du einen Schatz aus einem Opferschrein? Haust Du den Schrein zu Brei, um den richtigen Göttern wohl zu gefallen oder Krabbelst Du leise pfeifend vorüber und hoffst, dass nichts böses passiert?
Selbstverständlich wird in allen drei Fällen etwas schreckliches geschehen, nur die Art der Schrecklichkeit darfst Du bestimmen  ;-)

Und hier sind wir auch schon beim Tollsten an der ganzen Sache angekommen: Der Welt an sich!
Diese besteht nicht nur aus zahllosen Räumen und Türen in einer wundersam bedrohlichen Welt, auch viele Städte können bereist werden. Hier wird gehandelt, Passagiere oder neue Crewmitglieder an Bord genommen, Gerüchten gelauscht, Ränke geschmiedet, Proviant aufgeschnappt und vieles mehr.

Und jede Stadt, jeder kleine Ort am Wegesrand und jede zufällige Begegnung lassen Dich staunen, versetzen Dich in Schrecken oder entlocken Dir ein leises "wow". Die Welt ist dicht gewoben, es gibt viel zu sehen und noch mehr zu erforschen. 
Vom Ärztebund, der armen Patienten die Herzen stiehlt bis längst untergegangenen Städten, die aufs Neue erstehen ist alles dabei. Es ist ein Füllhorn aus Fantasie und Lovecraft´schem Schauermärchen. 
Wirklich alles ist hübsch gothisch angehaucht, düster romantisch und gruselig wundervoll zugleich. Da fühlt man sich sofort wohl und vor allem, da fühlt man sich gleich als Teil einer lebendigen, atmenden, pulsierenden Welt, die es zu entdecken gilt.

Und dieser Forscherdrang ists ja schließlich, der uns solcherlei Rogue Like Games zocken lässt, also geh schonmal an Bord, lass den Kessel heißlaufen und bringt Deinen Tausendfüßler auf Hochtouren, lieber Leser.

Ich wünsch Dir wie immer...

... viel Spaß, aber pass bloß auf, dass das Herz im Innern der Maschine nie aufhört zu schlagen, denn dann kommt sie, die Finsternis und bringt Dich um den Verstand...  ;-)

this game was an adventure. a house of many doors' writing is witty, hard-hitting, but also eloquent and charming, making use of this skill to create a vivid picture of its interesting and varied lore. i enjoyed doing all its quest lines- though a word of complaint is that their impacts seem to be short-lived (though that's perhaps an inevitable consequence of the game's format?). i sorely wish there were more interactions w companions bc i thoroughly enjoyed doing their quests and talking to them! (my personal favorites were cromlech, char, gladys, bishop and nicholas <3) and ofc, there's the tedium of crawling along the rooms, but that's easily remedied by hauling ass to ghoulwatch and stocking up on mirrors. 

this is a game of different choices and outcomes, and though i've sunk 60 hours enjoying much of what a house of many doors has to offer, the tediousness of how it plays sort of does discourage me to put in another 60 for a different playthrough. but i highly recommended playing through it at least once for the experience!

It's a little bit less polished than the sunless franchise, and much more focused on a linear story line, but the story itself is still great, and the plots you get wrapped up in are engaging.  The travel using the train can be somewhat meh - there's a lot of repetition of the sorts of events you encounter while exploring, and there aren't too many of them, but I would still recommend it on the basis of the story if you can get past that.

While this is a great effort for a very small indie company, I already played many hours of Failbetter Games' Sunless Sea and Sunless Skies so this feels like a bad knockoff. Unlike the SS games that have good tutorial mode and early-game missions to help you start making money and upgrading your crew, this just dumps you into things. And it doesn't help that the controls and menus are buggy and confusing. Given that FBG backed this guy, they should also have given him more assistance and advice.

Great story! Great companions, with their own personalities and side quests. The world is really fleshed out with an intense amount of imagination - absolutely anything could be in the next room. Yes it does have a few bugs and glitches but you can just power through them.
AHoMD delivery a world that is gripping, esoteric, and wonderfully crafted. 9/10

Pros: Amazing writing and pacing. Fantastic world-building. Pants-on-head bizarre at times, but also consistent.
Cons: Terrible combat (which you can allay for a good amount if you grind a bit for resources). Kind of buggy. 

If you want a game with a world that will suck you in for many, many hours, get this. Multiple endings, many approaches to take, and not rogue-like (which is a positive for some people).

I feel like this is a severely underrated game as far as the writing goes, and I wish the creator could give it some more love and maybe do a re-release in the future with better artistic & technical assets. I'm sending copies of it to my friends because for $2, it's just a steal. I'd honestly say it's worth $10 or so, I think I paid $20 several years ago and thought it was fair.

This is another game where I really wanted to like it, and gave it a few chances, but gave up after being more frustrated than anything else after an hour or two. The combat in particular is IMHO not fun. Maybe it does get more fun later on, but as it is it's either frustrating and unfortunately a bit too hard to avoid at times. 

The setting and atmosphere seem right up my alley, and probably the storyline is too but I just wasn't about to experience enough of it to enjoy it.

Это бриллиант. Мир на стыке стимпанка и сюрреализма, где маски носят лица, на черном рынке торгуют воспоминаниями, а из оболочек древних богов делают корабли. В плане нарратива в игре прекрасно все: квесты удивляют развитием сюжета, все персонажи наделены яркими личностями, а описания мира столь причудливы, что за его исследованием забываешь обо всем. Игра воспринимается в первую очередь как интерактивная книга. Язык автора богат, но чтобы сполна насладиться им, нужно ОЧЕНЬ хорошо знать английский язык — upper intermediate здесь не отделаешься.
С точки зрения геймплея игра про исследование и добычу ресурсов для этого самого исследования. А исследовать будет что и будет зачем – уж поверьте.
Арта в игре немного и он своеобразный, но хорошо работает на атмосферу. Музыка хорошая, хотя резкая смена дорожек порой заставляет поежиться.
Боевка в игре откровенно слабая и совершенно не интуитивная — рекомендую почитать в Интернете разъяснение ее механик, иначе ваше приключение может закончиться неожиданной фрустрацией. К счастью, бои занимают малую часть времени.

A House of Many Doors — это одна из лучших фантастических книг, которые мне довелось читать. И не нужно говорить, что это книга, а игра — она просто притворяется. Впрочем, с реиграбельностью и нелинейностью здесь все в порядке. Настоятельно рекомендую!
Enriching story and a unique world, easyily comprehensible gameplay make this worth your time. It could use more mirror pass short cuts in the late game to save time but that's about it.
Quality literature. Great art.
...I offered the corpse of a god to a murder of crows that responded by seducing me.

Игра была создана в рамках поддержки от Failbetter Games, так что присутствует ощущение сходства с Sunless Sea — и оно не ложное. Однако при этом перед нами всё же не клон, а отдельное полноценное произведение, просто подвергшееся влиянию и стилю, созданное в том же офисе. Одним человеком, что в моих глазах огромное достижение.

Это игра про огромный Дом, больше похожий на множество однотипных квадратных пещер, который в лучших традициях мира Fallen London ворует постройки, обитателей и даже богов других миров. И, естестественно, наше дело — тут приключаться (на многоногом поездообразном транспорте), вооружившись разной степени грандиозности целями. Например, сбежать из Дома (что, как везде твердят, безумие и невозможно). Или оставить после себя след (я, например, собираюсь открывать музей, пишу статьи и стихи — система их процедурной генерации весьма неплоха). Или поступить ещё как-то.

Сразу отмечу минус (для меня): боевая система. Она мне не понравилась вообще — это пошаговая стрельба в стиле Faster Than Light. Возможно, просто такое не для меня, потому я от всех потенциальных боёв, от которых можно откупиться, откупаюсь.

Картинка не то чтобы шедевральна — она специфична и в какой-то степени стильна, иллюстрации городов (подкреплённые описаниями, что важно) крайне атмосферны. Наполнение комнат, к сожалению, не блещет разнообразием и быстро приедается. А вот тексты на уровне — и требуют английского выше среднего, локализации нет; хотя по стилю, его разнообразию (а где надо — однообразию) всё же Sunless-серии мне больше понравились). Много разных историй — в стиле тех же Fallen London и Sunless-серии, есть дела вашей команды, есть политика, есть случайные события, в общем, можно найти чем заняться. В промежутке между чтением придётся просто переходить из одной не сильно отличающейся «комнаты» в другую, что не очень интересно.

И здесь можно быть добрым и помогать другим в значительно большей степени, чем в Sunless-серии. Меньше непосредственно безумия и отстранённости героя (и rogue-like элементов).

Так что если вы любите истории и не сильно фокусируетесь на активном игровом процессе — добро пожаловать в Дом.

The writing is amazing and deeply disturbing, and I mean that in the best way possible. While the combat minigame leaves something to be desired and moving between rooms can be monotonous, I had an extremely positive experience playing this game. If you're a fan of deeply narrative driven games, RPG elements, and cosmic horror, I'd highly recommend this. It covers so MUCH territory in its writing and it's really a wonderful experience. As a budding game writer, I was deeply inspired while playing and couldn't recommend it enough for people who want a unique interactive narrative experience.

When I get more time, I will come back write more for this. If this game for even a brief second catches the glimmer of your eye get it. The story is what sells this game alone and its world is the work of equal parts madness and genius. Without delving into spoilers, the  gameplay it’s self can be lack luster, but as a visual novel this game is a hidden gem.

I don't want to spoil the game so I guess I will leave my old review up, but with the new review and quality of life updates from the new update this game has only gotten better.

This game is unashamedly a total rip-off of Sunless Sea down to the minutest of details. It's been long since I've last wanted to play another game so badly after just a few minutes, as the little differences that are here, being a mind-numbingly boring overworld, lack of polish and obnoxious sound design, really add up to make an experience that feels vastly inferior to its contemporary from which it is stealing all its identity. Where other games improve upon their predecessors adding new ideas, refining gameplay concepts and improving quality of life, A House of Many Doors suffices with copying the bare minimum to make the Sunless Sea formula work without any knowledge of why it works. Stay away.

An interesting take on the interactive fiction genre, except that the author's literary style is like a grotesque carnival.
Every sentence is trying to deliver a punch, it gets a bit tiring after a while to read these long streams of deliberately obscure words, sometimes using french words for no reason, intrusive alliterations that make you think the author has a cargo-cult of actual literature.
Every character seems to be there just to deliver a zing, and before you get tired of the janky unescapable combats and quit the game, the word "edgy" will have traversed your mind a couple times.
If you liked sunless sea, you're definitely going to love this one. The exploring mechanics are janky, though.

Absolutely memorizing writing and atmosphere wrapped up in sub-par code. I would give ANYTHING for a mutli-million dollar remake of this game but I'm afraid it would lose its indie charm in the process.

When an absolutely great and genius narrative is objectively undermined by terrible, terrible code, you get A House of Many Doors. 

Gameplay and the art-style that you're going to see for 70% of your time is sub-par. 
What is truly exceptional is the cities, the places you happen to visit, their illustrations that can manage to both be sad and colorful and the writing, which is stellar.  No, seriously, it's incredibly good. The writer of this game made a couple of quests in Failbetter's Sunless Skies which are by far my favorite ones.  

It's honestly hard to recommend this game wholeheartedly, since at one point the game glitched in such a way that I found myself unable to lose sanity, which in a game that is all about getting lost in madness inside a devouring dimension sort of makes everything lose its edge. 

I still do, I mean, this is the work of one guy with some help by the people that made sunless sea. For what it is, it's an incredible achievement. 

It's just a shame it couldn't have been anything more, because man does this setting beg for a better made sequel.

Go into this with modest expectations of an indie game (mostly written and coded by one person) and you'll love it. Combat is silly. There are many bugs, and the game seems to reliably run out of memory and CTD after a few hours constant play, but with how forgiving the difficulty is and how easily you can save, this was never very frustrating and never cost much progress. 

The exploration is more lonely and repetitive than Sunless Seas (there is a fast travel system which helps a lot, look for some good Steam guides on gameplay tips). But the story is MUCH more memorable. You can have a tangible impact on the house around you, both in positive and negative ways. You get distinct crew-members to travel with, each of them with a unique side quest, many of which are fascinating and tie in unexpected ways to the main story-line. And there ihttps://store.steampowered.com/app/437250/A_House_of_Many_Doors/#s an overarching plot to the game with some very interesting endings. 

The story also seems to have more ... heart than Sunless Seas? There are as many twisted and gruesome things you can do to yourself and those around you in this game, but there are also a surprising number of kind deeds you can choose to do. Many of the story-lines revolve around in some way trying to help the other inhabitants of the house (in a very well-written way, where your original intentions may have unexpected and realistic outcomes). It made the game very enjoyable to role-play in!
If you like Sunless Sea, this is basically the same game with less polish but better stories.
The most imaginative game I've ever played.
